At a constant laboratory temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], newly hatched nauplii of Streptocephalus siamensis emerge from resting eggs at an age of 4 days [ab = 4 days], a developmental interval that aligns well with the rapid hatching times reported for other anostracan species inhabiting ephemeral pools. Upon emergence, the first free-swimming nauplius larva measures approximately 0.04 centimeters [Lb = approximately 0.04 centimeters] in total body length, a value inferred from comparative data on the closely related Phallocryptus spinosus. During this initial stage, the yolk-dependent embryo undergoes a swift transition to exogenous feeding, commencing filter feeding activity within the first day after hatching. This early onset of independent feeding is critical for growth in the temporary aquatic habitats typical of Southeast Asian fairy shrimp populations, where resource pulses are unpredictable and the growing season is brief. The nauplii progress through several instars, gradually increasing in size as they molt, and the external morphology shifts from the characteristic naupliar body plan toward the more elongated, segmented form of the adult.

The period of larval development culminates in a metamorphic moult, after which the post-metamorphic juvenile continues to grow and differentiate. This species exhibits a clear sexual size dimorphism, with adult females attaining a larger ultimate total length (2.13 centimeters) [Li = 2.13 centimeters] than their male counterparts (1.71 centimeters) [Li = 1.71 centimeters]. The maximum body size recorded in females reflects the high fecundity demands placed on ovigerous females, as a larger abdominal region provides greater capacity for carrying egg clutches. Males remain more compact, a morphological trait possibly linked to the energetic cost of clasping during the prolonged reproductive pairing typical of the genus. These length measurements, derived from laboratory-reared cohorts maintained under ad libitum feeding conditions, likely represent near-optimal growth trajectories. Under the same controlled thermal conditions, the post-larval transformation occurs within a tightly constrained window, and the growing juvenile molts at regular intervals to accommodate the rapid increase in body volume necessary to approach the adult asymptotic size.

Sexual maturation in Streptocephalus siamensis occurs after a relatively brief period following birth, with individuals typically reaching puberty at 8.5 days after birth [tp = 8.5 days after birth] when reared at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This accelerated maturation schedule, measured as the time since birth, is characteristic of species adapted to highly seasonal, temporary water bodies where the duration of habitat suitability is unpredictable. At this developmental juncture, the immature post-metamorphic crustacean begins gametogenesis and the first morphologically distinct secondary sex characteristics become apparent, allowing for reliable differentiation between males and females. The total body length recorded at the onset of this pubertal transition is approximately 1.3 centimeters [Lp = approximately 1.3 centimeters], a threshold size that appears to be necessary for the activation of the reproductive endocrine axis. Individuals that are smaller than this critical length at the corresponding age frequently exhibit delayed reproductive activation, suggesting a size-dependent gating mechanism for the onset of breeding activity that is common among branchiopod crustaceans.

Reproductive output in this branchiopod is substantial, with females producing approximately 200 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 200 eggs per clutch] and exhibiting a frequency of about 38 clutches per lifespan [F_R_i = about 38 clutches per lifespan] when maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The daily reproductive effort represents the maximum achievable rate, yielding approximately 262 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 262 eggs per day], as females in high-quality food environments release eggs in multiple clutches spread across the adult period. Under these conditions, gravid females carry subitaneous eggs in a well-developed brood pouch, and the eggs are released directly into the water column during each spawning event. This prodigious fecundity is an adaptation to the high mortality rates experienced by early life stages in the unpredictable, predator-rich temporary pond environment.

The complete lifespan of Streptocephalus siamensis at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] extends to approximately 37.7 days [am = approximately 37.7 days], after which natural mortality occurs due to senescence. Prior to death, the ultimate dry weight of an adult individual reaches about 0.0085 grams , a value estimated from allometric scaling relationships derived from Artemia salina, assuming a similar body composition. During the final days of life, reproductively active adults show a marked decline in feeding activity and swimming performance, followed by a progressive deterioration of physiological homeostasis and eventual organismal death. This abbreviated lifespan, typical of ephemeral-pool specialists, contrasts sharply with the multi-year life cycles of many marine crustaceans. The total energy allocated across the adult stage is largely directed toward the production of the massive egg complement, leaving limited reserves for somatic maintenance after the reproductive peak. Field observations suggest that this life-history strategy maximizes fitness in environments where habitat persistence is limited to a few weeks.
